4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	Read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions taken in it — and convert its friction into
9	changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer and less dependent on human steering. Read how the
10	work went; what the work committed is [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md)'s.
11	
12	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
13	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
14	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
15	
16	## The goal
17	
18	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
19	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
20	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
21	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
22	
23	## Where the conversation comes from
24	
25	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
26	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
27	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
28	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
29	  A small line-count `offset`/`limit` is not a safe way to `Read` the checked-out file: one JSONL line
30	  can be a single `tool_use`/`tool_result` running tens of thousands of characters, so even a short
31	  window can overflow the read cap. Check line lengths first (e.g. `awk '{print length}' <file> |
32	  sort -n | tail`) or condense the file with a script before attempting a raw read.
33	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
34	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
35	
36	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
37	when a session is done enough to mine.
38	
39	## What to look for — the friction signals
40	
41	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
42	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
43	
44	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
45	
46	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
47	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
48	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
49	
50	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
51	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
52	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
53	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
54	correctly **without the round-trip**.
55	
56	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
57	
58	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
59	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
60	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
61	convention and had it corrected in review.
62	
63	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
64	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
65	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
66	first, not after a detour.
67	
68	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
69	
70	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
71	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
72	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
73	
74	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
75	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
76	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
77	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
78	was already optimal.
79	
80	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
81	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
82	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
83	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
84	loss of quality.
85

87	
88	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
89	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
90	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
91	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the

94	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
95	
96	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
97	
98	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
99	
100	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
101	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
102	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
103	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
104	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
105

107	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
108	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
109	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
110	
111	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
112	
113	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
114	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
115	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
116	
117	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
118	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
119	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
120

124	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
125	silence it replaced.

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A schema property** — when the lesson is about a document's *shape*: a field that must be present, a
59	   value from a closed set, a type, a key set nothing may extend. It belongs in the JSON Schema the document
60	   points at with `$schema` (created from the first such rule where the document has none), which an editor
61	   shows while the document is written and the engine's `schema-conformance` check enforces for every such
62	   document at once. Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there: a declared `checkParsedFiles`
63	   assertion over a field, or a coded rule re-reading a document's shape by hand, is a schema check in
64	   disguise. Only what a schema cannot say — a relation between two documents, a value that depends on the
65	   tree — goes on to the rungs below.
66	2. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
67	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. Declare it at the moment its signature
68	   lives: a **world** check over the tree — one pass ("these patterns over these files"), or two when a value
69	   read in one place must agree with, exist in or be absent from another (`extractValueSets` derives the set,
70	   `checkSetValues`/`checkSetPairs`/`requireIdenticalFiles` quantify over it); a **work** check over the
71	   change (`scope: "work"` — the lines it adds or removes, a co-change, an untracked file, the session's
72	   declared comment classes); or an **action** guard on a tool call (`scope: "action"`, `guardToolCalls` —
73	   denied or nudged at PreToolUse, backstopped over the transcript at Stop). Most captured conditions are
74	   one of these, and a lesson about *how an operation is performed* is usually the third. Give it
75	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
76	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
77	   else's next change, not this run's.
78	3. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
79	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
80	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
81	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
82	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
83	4. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure or a bias rather than a condition —
84	   and name the moment it must load under its `metadata`: `force-load-on-file-edits-paths`,
85	   `force-load-on-tool-calls` (opening a PR, committing, merging, fetching), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`
86	   (an owner's command phrase) or `force-load-on-tool-results-matching` (a symptom in a result). A skill
87	   with no trigger loads on description alone, which is model discretion; a procedure keyed to an act has a
88	   call to name, and rules sharing a trigger belong in one skill so one load carries the whole procedure.
89	5. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
90	
91	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
92	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
93	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
94	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
95	
96	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
97	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
98	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
99	
100	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
101	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small** — a pass adds at most two rules, each one
102	sentence. How a rule is phrased and sized, and where its rationale goes — the brief rule in `RULES.md`, the
103	reaffirmable reason in the pack's `references.md` — is the
104	[writing-pack-prose](skills/writing-pack-prose/SKILL.md) skill's; load it before writing any. The full
105	evidence trail stays in the PR body and the issue.
106	
107	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
108	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
109	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
110	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
111	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
112	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
113	
114	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
115	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
116	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
117	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
118	basics pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
119	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
120	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
121	
122	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
123	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
124	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
125	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
126	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
127	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
128	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
129	
130	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
131	
132	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
133	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
134	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
135	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

A repo serving a static tree from Cloudflare Workers static assets on its own
domain gets the whole deployment from the canon: the nightly site-release task
(preflight the claimed hostnames, cut the version, stamp the pages, push the
bump, upload, report what the domain answered), the version scheme itself, four
checks over the upload boundary, the version stamp, the beacon token and the
single path to production, the releasing-a-cloudflare-site skill, and the
Cloudflare account's own steps as adoptionHandover.

The previous host's leftovers are evaluated rather than listed: an inherited
CNAME or a GitHub Pages address on a claimed hostname is resolved in public DNS
before a version is consumed, and a workflow or CNAME file still publishing is a
check's finding — so no adopter reads a checklist of steps that are no-ops for
them.

Generalized out of ClaudiniteWebsite's local pack: the published tree, the
claimed hostnames and the analytics loader all come from the repo's own wrangler
config and the placeholder a published file carries, so the pack asks its
adopters nothing.

The forced-wake block re-read the queue over the network and planned from
that read alone. GitHub's issue list is eventually consistent, so the read
missed the standing item the ops above had just filed, and the force minted
a second one beside it: on Shepherd a forced `claudinite-lifecycle/update`
filed #577 and then #582 fifteen seconds later, and both claimed an executor.

This is the failure mode #1340 already fixed for the drain gate four lines
further down, and the comment on `readied` in this very function states it
outright. The wake block was the one site in `runScheduler` still trusting
the read — and the site where a miss writes a duplicate rather than skipping
a dispatch.

So the wake plans over the same union the gate's verdict is: what the list
returned, plus what this run created. `withOwnWrites` adds only what the read
missed, leaving a read that is ahead of the run's own record intact.

The sim models `force` against its own in-memory issue list, so it asserts
the intended behaviour and cannot reproduce this; the regression sits beside
drain-gate.test.mjs instead, against a list read that has not caught up.

Closes #1979

{"total_count":1,"incomplete_results":false,"items":[{"author_association":"OWNER","body":"## Problem

A class of pack rules only matters while editing files in one folder (product-wiki's `RULES.md` is the exemplar: ten rules about writing wiki pages, paid for by every session in every declaring repo). A skill is the right home, but loading it is model discretion, and the only enforcement available today is a post-hoc `check_the_work` finding, which fires after the agent has already gone in a direction the skill would have prevented.

## Change

- A manifest field, `skillsBeforeEditing`: `[{ files: <glob>, skill: <name> }]`, validated by the pack schema; the skill must be one the pack bundles.
- The engine's PreToolUse hook widens from `Bash` to file-editing tools too. On `Edit`/`Write`/`NotebookEdit` it matches the path against the active packs' declarations and, when the transcript shows no load of the named skill, denies the call with a reason naming the skill. Loaded: allow, zero cost.
- A `check_the_work` backstop: files in the diff match a declaration and the transcript shows no load. Covers edits made through Bash, which the hook cannot see.
- product-wiki: the editing rules move into a skill declared for `product-wiki/**`, the weekly task loads it by name, and `RULES.md` keeps only the rules about reading (the sink is human-reviewed; consult the wiki when working on requirements).
- claudinite-growth's `writing-pack-prose` becomes the second caller, for pack `RULES.md`/`SKILL.md` files.

  "severity": "advisory",
  "scope": "action",
  "since": "2026-09-06",
  "failureMessage": "git checkout -- restores from the index, destroying uncommitted work as thoroughly as the mutation it undoes",
  "guardToolCalls": [

      "tool": "Bash",
      "inputField": "command",
      "match": "/(^|[;&|]\\s*|\\n\\s*)git\\s+(checkout\\s+--|restore\\s|stash\\b)/",
      "what": "a working-tree restore: \"{match}\"",
      "fix": "commit or stage the real edit first, and only mutate a file whose current state you are ready to throw away"

    }

}

382://   guardToolCalls     [{ tool, inputField, match, requireMatch, unlessMatches,
383-//                         inputMatches, unlessInputMatches, inputFieldAbsent,
384-//                         atMostPerSession, what, fix }]
385-//                      `tool` is the tool's exact name or a regex over names
386-//                      (/^mcp__github__(list|search)_/). The entry fires on a
387-//                      call to it when every condition it declares holds and
388-//                      no unless-condition does: `match` hits the value at
389-//                      `inputField` (a dot path into the tool's input, read as
390-//                      text) / `requireMatch` MISSES it / `inputMatches` hits
391-//                      the whole input serialized as JSON / some field named
392-//                      in `inputFieldAbsent` is missing / this is the call past
393-//                      `atMostPerSession` earlier calls of the tool in this
394-//                      session with the same `inputField` value (the same
395-//                      whole input, without one). {tool}, {field} (the field's
396-//                      text) and {match} interpolate
397-//
398-// The reference-barrier assertion — a directed folder-access graph enforced by
399-// the reference-scanning engine (helpers/reference-scanning.mjs, which owns the
400-// edge vocabulary's semantics):
401-//   forbidReferences   [{ from | between | siblings, to, scope, allow, except,
402-//                         matchNames, alsoMatchNames, matchUniqueFilenames,
403-//                         reason }]
404-//                      each entry one barrier edge, normalized at load (a
405-//                      malformed edge is an authoring error); the rule's
406-//                      failureMessage is the why (an edge's `reason` overrides
407-//                      it), and a rule-level `fix` replaces the engine's
408-//                      composed crossing remedy
409-//
410-// The markdown-section assertions read each scanned page's `## ` sections —
411-// headings matched case-insensitively with suffix words allowed, fenced code
412-// blocks invisible, a section running to the next `## ` heading or EOF. A
413-// top-level bullet is a column-0 `-`/`*`/`+` line; a bullet BLOCK is the bullet
414-// plus its indented continuation lines; a DATED bullet leads with its
415-// YYYY-MM-DD run date, bold or plain, validated as a real calendar date. Every
416-// assertion except requirePresent asserts nothing when the section is absent
417-// (presence is its own declared finding, never double-reported):
418-//   checkSections      [{ section | sections: [names], … }] with, each optional:
419-//                        requirePresent                   the `## {section}` heading must exist
420-//                        requireFirstOnPage               no other `## ` heading may precede it
421-//                                                         ({first} = the heading that does)
422-//                        forbidProseLines                 non-bullet, non-continuation lines
423-//                                                         are findings ({line} = the text)
424-//                        eachBulletBlockMatches           { pattern } — every bullet block must match
425-//                        eachBulletLeadsWithDate          { whenUndated, whenNotRealDate } —
426-//                                                         every bullet starts with a real date
427-//                                                         ({date} = the one that isn't)
428-//                        minBullets / maxBullets          { count } — bullet-count floor/ceiling
429-//                                                         ({bullets} = the actual count)
430-//                        maxBulletBlockLength             { characters } — block-length ceiling
431-//                                                         ({characters} = the actual length)
432-//                        newestDatedBulletWithinDays      { days } — the newest dated bullet
433-//                                                         (dates > 2 days in the future
434-//                                                         discarded; clock = ctx.now, wall
435-//                                                         clock otherwise) must be at most
436-//                                                         `days` old ({age}, {date}, {days})
437-//                      {bullet} everywhere = the bullet line's first 80 characters
438-//
439-// `what`/`fix` are templates: `{path}`, a named capture group's `{name}`, and
440-// `{match}` (a matchLines hit's text), `{lines}`/`{limit}` (maxLines) interpolate.
441-//
442-// LEGACY SPELLINGS, accepted but not for new declarations (a member's own

### 125f40a Refuse to answer --list or --init from a partial pack registry (#2021)
discoverPacks never throws when a pack fails to load: a pack.mjs whose
import raises, a rule module that will not load and an unparseable
declared-checks.json all land on its `errors` array, and the pack is simply
absent from `packs`. A caller that reads one without the other cannot tell a
pack that was never there from one that did not load.

Both --list and --init read only `packs`. So --list printed a catalog short
by however many packs failed and exited 0, which is how a dropped pack
reached CI as an unrelated missing check rather than as its own error. --init
had it worse: it seeds a declaration a member copies once and never again, so
a pack absent at that moment is absent from that repo's settings for good.

Both now refuse. The reason goes to stderr, naming each pack and its error,
so --list's stdout stays the machine-readable channel a caller parses and a
short catalog can never be mistaken for a complete one.

The catalog test carries stderr into its own failure message too. A check
missing from the catalog is a pack that did not load, and that channel is the
only place the reason is written; without it the assertion reports which id
was absent and discards the run's explanation of why.

This makes the failure legible, not impossible — what makes a pack's import
fail under parallel load is still unknown, and is why the flake was filed
from symptoms. The next occurrence now names the pack and the error instead
of a regex that did not match.

Closes #2008

### 522b8ec Dashboard: move the page's modules under src/, split by layer (#2007)
* Dashboard: move the page's modules under src/, split by layer

The pack kept 33 .mjs files flat at its root beside index.html, the schema and
the manifest. The import graph carried the whole structure — what the browser
loads, what is node-only, what is pure derivation, what draws DOM — and the
folder tree carried none of it.

  src/app.mjs     the entry index.html names
  src/derive/     pure: facts in, rows and figures out (11)
  src/read/       the I/O plane: credential, client, cache, readers (10)
  src/render/     shared visual vocabulary and drawing primitives (4)
  src/views/      the two pages (2)
  tooling/        node-only: serve, build-site, deployment-config,
                  oauth-exchange (4)

index.html, the icons, the schema, the example config, pack.mjs and the two
markdown files stay at the pack root; test/, docs/, tasks/, worldRules/ and
stubs/ stay put, being directory names the vendoring walk and the task runner
know.

Depth stops at one level under src/: file-placement counts a reference at
folder distance three or more as a reach, and sibling layer folders are two.

Everything the browser loads now sits under one directory, so build-site
decides what to publish by naming `tooling/` rather than by a list of
filenames to keep in step.

The staged-import test walked only the page root, which no longer holds a
module; it now walks the whole staged tree and resolves each specifier against
its own file's directory — a stricter check than the one it replaces.

Refs #2005

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01KwFn2kmKLiXYHxo3d2vWLu

* Dashboard: move index.html under src/ too, keeping its served URL

src/ held every module the browser loads except the page itself. It now holds
the page too, and the dashboard's URL does not move: it is still served at
packs/claudinite-dashboard/, one directory above where the file is stored.

An HTML `src=` resolves against the document's URL rather than the file's path,
so the page's script tag keeps naming ./src/app.mjs and its icon ./favicon.svg
— correct at the URL it is served from, wrong relative to the directory it sits
in. Opening the file directly, or serving src/ as a root, breaks every module
it loads, so the file says so at its top and only two places serve it:

  serve.mjs      a directory request resolves to the page under src/
  build-site.mjs stages it by MOVING it up to the served root, never copying,
                 so no second broken entry is left at src/index.html

dashboard.config.json and favicon.svg stay at the pack root, beside the served
page rather than inside the source tree — verified live: the config fetch still
resolves to packs/claudinite-dashboard/dashboard.config.json.

Both failure modes are pinned by `the staged tree mirrors the mount, with the
root a redirect`, and both were watched failing: a copy instead of a move, and
no relocation at all.

Refs #2005

  larger one many module headers cite by section, were decided separately rather than

  nothing executes from the mount — forcing delivery buys noise rather than assurance; forcing

  nightly converge stops being the reliable delivery path.

  grows tells you nothing today, and the honest version is what happened in a window — this

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

   had a green dispatch run beside a gated phantom and merged on the next cycle. Retire the rule if
   that setting stops gating same-repo bot PRs, or if the queue stops dispatching its own runs.
+- **(RULES-83)** Owner, 2026-09-06 (#1814, session cd625226): "The whole point of Claudenite is to
+  install on the repo. Claude code plugins help users. Claudinite helps repositories. Repos run
+  their own tasks, repos implemet using their skills and rules. Repos validate state based on
+  checks. The direction is not Claude Plugins." The commercialization draft had been built around
+  Claude Code's plugin/marketplace system and costed an un-vendoring refactor that exists only
+  under a per-user framing; the correction forced a second whole-document rework in one session.
+  `docs/commercialization/DESIGN.md` states the same premise but carries a "not implemented"
+  banner disclaiming itself as a description of the repository, so nothing a session reads by
+  default carried it. Retire the rule if Claudinite ever ships a per-user or per-machine install
+  path alongside the repository one.
+- **(RULES-84)** Merging #1815, 2026-09-10 (session cd625226): the branch had sat open since
+  2026-09-06, 68 commits behind, and `merge_pull_request` returned `405 Pull Request has merge
+  conflicts`. Both `git merge origin/main` and `git rebase origin/main` conflicted in exactly one
+  file — `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/declared-checks.json` — where `main` had edited a
+  neighbouring entry after the branch appended its own, so the whole-file JSON rewrite collided
+  with a change the branch had no opinion about. Taking the base file with `git checkout --ours`
+  and re-appending the single entry resolved it in one pass; the detour cost ~90s and a merge
+  abort. Several auto-merging runs a day append to this file, so the collision is structural.
+  Retire the rule if the file stops being appended by more than one run at a time.
+- **(RULES-85)** #1934, 2026-09-11: `update` declared `supersede_existing_pr`, so a member that
+  could not land — slow CI, a `needs-human` park, a review gate — collected one obsolete update
+  pull request a night, and the one that actually needed attention was never the one in front of
+  anybody. Its converge is a full recompute from the base, which is exactly what makes rewriting
+  the standing pull request correct rather than lossy. Retire the rule if a task appears whose
+  successive runs produce genuinely unrelated answers, where the earlier pull request is worth
+  keeping open beside the new one.
+- **(RULES-86)** #1934, 2026-09-11: the same converge recomputes the same tree from the same base
+  every night, so reusing the pull request would have force-pushed an identical answer onto it
+  each cycle; each force-push gives the pull request a new head and discards the checks that had
+  already run, which on a member waiting for slow CI is the difference between eventually landing
+  and never landing. `worker.mjs` compares trees rather than commits because this cycle's commit
+  is new by construction — its own timestamp — and only the content decides whether anything is
+  owed. Retire the rule if GitHub stops keying check runs to the head sha.
+- **(check:busy-wait-loop)** Session 4baa0098, 2026-09-11 16:12–16:15Z: after the #1933 merge the
+  session backgrounded `capture-log.mjs`, then waited on its output file with
+  `until [ -s <file> ]; do :; done`. The file was never written, the empty body never yielded, and
+  the loop ran 2m28s until the owner killed the task — asking "What is holding you?" twice before
+  the session could answer at all. The retry that worked ran the command in the foreground into a
+  file. `bare-sleep-wait` catches the opposite spelling (a wait with no condition) and would not
+  have fired here. Retire the check if the harness starts pre-empting a wedged Bash call.
+- **(check:mount-path-in-the-canon-home)** 14 sessions across the captured corpus ran an engine
+  module through `.claudinite/shared/…` from this repo's root and got `Cannot find module` —
+  `check_the_work`/`check_the_world` mostly, but `converge-item.mjs` and
+  `session-end-command.mjs` too, and twice on 2026-09-13 alone (sessions 809b13de and f44b0ffb).
+  The mount path is what `claudinite-lifecycle`'s rules and the queue's instructions spell,
+  correctly, for a member; the canon home has no `.claudinite/shared/` at all, so the sweep a
+  session believed it ran never ran until it noticed the error and retried. Replayed over 558
+  sessions rooted here the guard fires on those 14 and nothing else — the `cd` into a cloned
+  member or a scratch consumer tree, the two-root `||` fallback, and the path quoted inside a
+  heredoc all stay silent. Retire the check if the canon ever vendors itself.
+- **(RULES-87)** #1951, 2026-09-13: an unshipped `pr_name` field refused to be declared beside
+  `automerge` other than `"nothing"`, beside `supersede_existing_pr`, and beside
+  `no_code_changes` — three restrictions reasoned from what a pull request two tasks shared
+  might do to a sibling task's work, none of them asked for. The owner's correction: the
+  properties are orthogonal, a pull request tries to auto-merge regardless and simply stays open
+  when its policy does not cover the diff, and an interaction between properties is the owner's
+  call to permit rather than the author's to infer. The next cut rebuilt the same coupling in
+  prose — a schema description stating the new field meant one standing pull request, true only
+  beside `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` — so the rule reaches the description as well as the
+  validator. Scoped to NEW properties because the contract already carries three grandfathered
+  pairs, named in the rule. The field itself was dropped (#1950) for having no user; the rule is
+  what the episode was worth. Retire the rule if a property is introduced whose legal values
+  genuinely cannot be enumerated without a sibling's.
+
+- **(RULES-88)** #2015, 2026-09-13: owner review of `commitFiles` and `windowCommits`, both
+  readers — "when a function is named `<verb><noun>` that usually conveys that it performs that
+  action on that noun. You have a READER of the committed files here, right?" Retire only if the
+  corpus stops naming readers by their noun.
+
+- **(check:shell-write-to-skill-scoped-path)** `pretooluse-judge.mjs` holds an edit until its
+  path-scoped skill is loaded, but only for `Edit`, `Write` and `NotebookEdit`; #1648 accepted
+  the Stop-time backstop for shell writes, which the hook cannot see. Across 2026-09-13's
+  captures, thirteen attended sessions made 1755 Bash calls and twelve of them made **no** file-tool
+  call at all — every repo edit went through `cat >`, `python3 - <<PY` or `sed -i` — and ten
+  collected a blocking `skill-loaded-before-editing` finding at Stop, each costing a load and a
+  re-review of work already written. Advisory rather than blocking because a bulk sweep across
+  many scoped files is a legitimate shell job the guard cannot tell apart. Retire the check if
+  the pre-edit guard learns to read Bash.

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The branch and the pull request were chosen for you
11	
12	**Push to the `Target-branch:` your item carries, and onto the `Target-pr:` where it
13	carries one.** The executor resolved both from the task's `expected_outcome` before
14	your session started: `fresh_pr` gave you a new branch and left the task's earlier pull
15	requests alone; `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` gave you the branch of the task's
16	newest open pull request when it had no conflicts, and a fresh one otherwise;
17	`supersede_existing_pr` gave you a fresh branch and listed the earlier ones under
18	`Supersedes:`. Where there is a `Target-pr:`, push onto it and open nothing — the pull
19	request already exists and your push updates it. Where there is none, open your pull
20	request on that branch. Never mint a branch name, never search for an open pull
21	request to reuse, and never close an earlier run's pull request yourself: the converge
22	(`converge-item.mjs`, handed `--pr`) closes what `Supersedes:` names once yours
23	exists, and a run that delivered nothing leaves them where they were.
24	
25	## Say which task wrote it
26	
27	**Every commit you push on a task's behalf carries `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on
28	its own line** — the pack and task id from the work item's first line. When you merge,
29	put the same line in the squash commit's message too: the merge commit is what lands on
30	the default branch, and it is the one the signal collectors read.
31	
32	That trailer is how the scheduler tells the project moving from the machinery running. A
33	task's own delivery must never count as the repo activity that wakes the next task, and
34	a title is not a reliable way to say so — every new task's title is a new leak. Yours
35	says it in the commit.
36	
37	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
38	
39	Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
40	`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `fresh_pr` with `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as
41	`fresh_pr` with `anything`; `none` and `pr` read as `no_code_changes` and `fresh_pr`).
42	On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
43	read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
44	`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
45	Whichever source it came from:
46	
47	- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
48	  applies to you.
49	- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
50	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
51	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
52	- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder
53	  scope such as `['under:product-wiki']`, or an intersection of the two,
54	  `['under:product-wiki && doc-changes']`) — the task may
55	  land its PR only when the diff sits inside the policy, and the policy engine decides
56	  that, never your reading of the diff. Before step 2, run it from the repository root —
57	  `merge-policy.mjs` at the root of the claudinite-tasks pack (probe
58	  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs`, falling back to
59	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs` in the canon):
60	
61	  ```
62	  node <that file> --base <the PR's base branch> --policy '<the terms, ;-joined>'
63	  ```
64	
65	  `AUTOMERGE: no` — leave the PR open for review, quote the verdict line in your wrap-up,
66	  and stop; a diff wider than its policy waiting for a person is a correct outcome, and
67	  you never re-shape a change to fit the classifier. `AUTOMERGE: yes` — amend your
68	  branch's final commit to carry the arming trailer on its own line,
69	  `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy: <the same expression>`, push, and continue below (the
70	  `automerge-policy-scope` check re-measures the diff against the trailer, so a
71	  mis-measured arm goes red instead of merging).
72	
73	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
74	
75	`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
76	
77	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
78	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
79	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading an
80	  authorized landing to review is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
81	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
82	  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
83	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
84	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
85	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.
86	
87	## 2. Arm auto-merge
88	
89	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
90	it once this repo's required checks pass.
91	
92	## 3. When the arm is rejected
93	
94	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
95	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
96	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
97	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
98	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
99	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
100	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
101	  PR's **head sha**:
102	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
103	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
104	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
105	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
106	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
107	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
108	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
109	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
110	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
111	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
112	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the ceiling — the trail
113	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
114	    unseen check does not survive anything.
115	
116	## Never
117	
118	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
119	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
120	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
121	are always legal outcomes.

your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.

carries one.** The executor resolved both from the task's `expected_outcome` before
your session started: `fresh_pr` gave you a new branch and left the task's earlier pull

newest open pull request when it had no conflicts, and a fresh one otherwise;

## Say which task wrote it

its own line** — the pack and task id from the work item's first line. When you merge,
put the same line in the squash commit's message too: the merge commit is what lands on

That trailer is how the scheduler tells the project moving from the machinery running. A
task's own delivery must never count as the repo activity that wakes the next task, and
a title is not a reliable way to say so — every new task's title is a new leak. Yours
says it in the commit.

## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest

Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `fresh_pr` with `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as

On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
Whichever source it came from:

- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
  applies to you.
- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder

  `merge-policy.mjs` at the root of the claudinite-tasks pack (probe
  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs`, falling back to
  `packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs` in the canon):

  ```
  node <that file> --base <the PR's base branch> --policy '<the terms, ;-joined>'
  ```

  you never re-shape a change to fit the classifier. `AUTOMERGE: yes` — amend your

  mis-measured arm goes red instead of merging).

- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/committing

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.
- **Reference the issue** — `Refs #n`, or `Fixes #n` / `Closes #n` where the commit finishes it;
  the `task-lifecycle` check reads it off the branch.
- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.
- **Stage by name** — `git add <paths>` for the files this commit is about; `-a` sweeps in whatever
  else was in progress.

input.title: Claudinite growth: extract lessons
input.body:
Window: the thirteen substantive commits of 2026-09-14's run (#2026), the pull requests they landed, and the captures on `conversation-logs` for the last 24 hours plus the first 24 hours still on the branch (2026-07-19/20, the hindsight pass).

## What landed — one check, no prose

`shell-write-to-skill-scoped-path`, an **advisory** action guard in `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite`.

**The friction.** `engine/hooks/pretooluse-judge.mjs:45` holds a file edit until its path-scoped skill is loaded — but `FILE_TOOLS` is `Edit`, `Write`, `NotebookEdit` only. #1648 designed it that way and accepted a `check_the_work` backstop for "edits made through Bash, which the hook cannot see". The measurement says that backstop is now the common path, not the exception:

| | |
|---|---|
| attended sessions captured on 2026-09-13 | 13 |
| Bash calls across them | 1755 |
| sessions making **zero** `Edit`/`Write`/`NotebookEdit` calls | 12 |
| sessions collecting a blocking `skill-loaded-before-editing` finding at Stop | 10 |

Every repo edit in those sessions went through `cat > packs/…/RULES.md`, `python3 - <<'PY'` or `sed -i`, so the skill requirement arrived at Stop — after the work it was there to shape — and each finding cost a load plus a re-read of what had already been written. The unattended queue sessions in the same window used `Edit` heavily (7–22 calls each) and collected none.

**The guard.** A Bash `command` whose text puts a write construct — a `>`/`>>` redirect, an `open(`/`Path(`, or a quoted assignment — directly in front of a path the corpus scopes to a skill (`*.test.*`, `RULES.md`, `SKILL.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `tasks/**`, `engine/checks/**`). Its `fix` is the one-line remedy: write it with `Write`, or `Edit` after a read.

**Tuning is measured, not guessed.** The regex was run against the window's own 1755 captured commands: 93 hits, of which one is a read (`taskPath="packs/basics/tasks/…/task.md"` inside a `node -e` `existsSync`). Two earlier drafts were rejected by that corpus — an unprefixed path alternation fired on `grep --include=RULES.md`, and a bare `VAR=path` branch fired on three `sed -n` reads.

**Advisory rather than blocking**, deliberately: a bulk sweep across many scoped files (the 2026-09-13 `rules-line-length` reflow is the window's own example) is a legitimate shell job this regex cannot tell from a single-file rewrite, and denying it would wedge real work. The rationale and its retirement condition are in `references.md`.

**Red-first.** The guard was weakened (prefix group emptied, `RULES.md`/`SKILL.md`/`CLAUDE.md` dropped) and the fixture went red at `2 !== 4`; restoring it returned 7/7. The negative half of the fixture is the window's own commonest shell shapes — a suite run redirected to the scratchpad, a `node --test` on a scoped path, a `grep --include=RULES.md`.

## What did not land

- **The activity half yielded nothing new.** #2021's "a caller reading `packs` without `errors` cannot tell absent from failed-to-load" is the local pack's existing *"a worker crash sharing a benign outcome code"* rule; #2022's "state the conditional cache form inline instead of naming another pack's stub" is `claudinite-growth`'s RULES-2; #2015's per-run memo and #2007's `src=` resolution are a truism and a one-call-site gotcha respectively.
- **The owner's review comments in the window were already captured** — `<verb><noun>` naming (RULES-88), "don't talk about other extensions in the rules" (growth RULES-2), property orthogonality (RULES-87).
- **The hindsight pass (2026-07-19/20)** re-read six captures. Its dominant signal was `comment-classification` firing at Stop in all six; that rule is long since in `basics/RULES.md` and the check no longer fires. Nothing survived.
- **The prose ration went unspent.** No `RULES.md` rule this run, so the `prose-to-checks` upgrade pass had an empty scope.

## Suite

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` → 3537/3544. The seven failures are pre-existing and unrelated to this diff: six in `packs/claude-code-web-users-support/test/session-start.test.mjs`, which inherits `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED=0` from any unattended session and passes 9/9 under `env -u` (filed separately), and `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs`'s deliberate shallow-clone assertion. `check_the_world` is clean.

Closes #2026

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (min 1, max 100)

input.title: session-start.test.mjs reads the ambient CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED, so the suite is red in every unattended session
input.body:
## What happens

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` from an unattended session reports 7 failures. Six are in `packs/claude-code-web-users-support/test/session-start.test.mjs`:

```
not ok 970 - the store is read locally when this tree IS the store
not ok 971 - a declared path is honoured, not just the default
not ok 972 - no file for this person is a soft note, never a halt
not ok 974 - no usable identity means there is nothing to look up
not ok 976 - the loaded preferences are weighed onto the engine facet channel
not ok 977 - prose weighs the same as bullets — the window does not care about markup

The input did not match the regular expression /MY PREFS/. Input:
'USER PREFERENCES: the session is unattended (CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED=0) …'
```

The same file passes 9/9 under `env -u CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED node --test packs/claude-code-web-users-support/test/session-start.test.mjs`.

## Why

#1991 gated the preference load on `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED`. The cases that exercise a *loaded* preference set the store path and the identity but leave that variable to the ambient environment, so the session-start step correctly refuses to load and the assertions about what it loaded fail.

The harness sets `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED=0` in exactly the sessions the task queue runs in, so the repo's own suite is red for every unattended run and green for a person at a terminal and for CI. That asymmetry is the cost: an unattended session cannot tell its own regression from this one, and the honest move — reporting a red suite — reads as noise.

## Fix

Have each case state the attendance it means rather than inherit it: set `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED` explicitly on the cases that expect a load (and keep the existing unattended case, which should set it too). Nothing about the gate itself is wrong.

_Filed by the Claudinite task `claudinite-growth/growth-extract`, running as work item missingbulb/Claudinite#2026 — no person asked for this issue._
